lesson.title: The Multiplier Behind Every Increase: Growth Factor
lesson.summary: The growth factor is the number greater than 1 that you multiply by each time period in an exponential growth model, and it packages a constant percent increase into a single number.
lesson.body:
In the exponential growth equation y equals a times b raised to the t, the number b controls whether the quantity grows and how fast. When b is greater than 1, the quantity grows every period, and b itself has a name: the growth factor. The growth factor tells you exactly what you multiply the previous amount by to get the next amount.

Growth factors are closely tied to percent increase. If a quantity increases by r percent each period, written as a decimal, the growth factor is b equals 1 plus r. The 1 represents keeping 100 percent of what you already had, and the r represents the extra percent added on top. For example, a 4 percent increase has a growth factor of 1.04, a 10 percent increase has a growth factor of 1.10, and a 50 percent increase has a growth factor of 1.5. If something exactly doubles each period, its growth factor is 2, since doubling means keeping the original 100 percent and adding another 100 percent. A growth factor must be strictly greater than 1 for actual growth to occur: a growth factor of exactly 1 means no change at all, and a positive number less than 1 describes decay instead, which is the subject of the next two chapters.

Here is a worked example. A town has a population of 12,000 people and is growing at a steady 4 percent per year, so its growth factor is 1.04. The model is P(t) equals 12,000 times 1.04 raised to the t, where t is years from now. To predict the population in 5 years, build up the powers of 1.04 step by step: 1.04 squared equals 1.0816. Multiplying by 1.04 again, 1.0816 times 1.04 equals 1.124864. Again, 1.124864 times 1.04 equals 1.16985856. One more time, 1.16985856 times 1.04 equals 1.2166529024. Now multiply by the initial population: 12,000 times 1.2166529024 equals 14,599.83, which rounds to about 14,600 people after 5 years.

Notice something important about that growth: the population is not gaining a fixed 480 people every year (4 percent of the original 12,000). Instead, each year it gains 4 percent of that year's larger population, so the actual number of new people added grows a little every year even though the percent stays exactly the same. That is the defining feature of a constant growth factor, and it is exactly the mechanism behind compound interest and the linear versus exponential comparison covered in later chapters.
